dossier.summary: The paper asks how accurate the neighbour-fraction OLS estimator of the global average treatment effect is under network interference, using a large simulation (1622 cells, six graphs, several outcome mechanisms and designs) with exactly known truth. Its core results are well supported by the delivered result files, from which the numbers in its text and tables reproduce apart from small rounding slips: a closed-form bias gamma(s-1) that matches 144 noiseless cells, bias that does not shrink with n, an SD that scales as sqrt(d/n) on ER graphs, a 5.5-18.6x SD price against the difference in means, and under-coverage of dependence-ignoring intervals. The abstract overstates two conclusions: bias dominates under nonlinear spillover in only about a third of concave/convex cells (none under cluster designs), and tuned boosting does help for sigmoid truth. Several appendix details do not match the files or code: the Stanford3 coverage values average OLS(z,f) with the correctly specified regression, a Hajek bias range was typed into a note rather than computed, and the two-hop strength differs from the code. The record shows a mostly transparent process (post-hoc thresholds and post-freeze grids are disclosed, no estimator touches the truth), except that one first-freeze decision rule was rewritten while its result was known, which the paper does not acknowledge. Reproduction from the delivery is partial because the figure/table scripts and the raw per-replicate data are not included.

claims.quote: Under Bernoulli($p$) assignment and one-hop spillover, the population bias is $\gamma(s-1)$ for an exactly computable $s$; it matches 144 noiseless cells within Monte-Carlo error
does not shrink with $n$ ($+2.53\to+2.49$ from $n=10^3$ to $2\cdot10^4$), is proportional to the interference strength in 14 of 16 tested groups, and changes sign with $p$
On Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs the standard deviation scales as $n^{-0.501\pm0.005}d^{0.495\pm0.006}$.
At the grid's $(n,d,\sigma)$ the estimator beats the difference in means once interference is moderate, but has 5.5--18.6 times its SD when there is none
the crossover strength scales as $n^{-0.49}d^{1.01}$ and the SD ratio as $d^{1.0}$
richer fits (penalised OLS, tuned boosting) do not help
intervals that ignore dependence under-cover, and a cluster bootstrap does not reach 95\% either
Heavy-tailed degrees raise neither SD nor bias in a matched test
the Stanford3 case where graph clusters hurt replicates on a second seed
this is the cost of extrapolating to the corners, not of misspecification
The regression-based GATE estimator is accurate when its exposure model is right and the interference is not weak, and its failure is mostly a \emph{bias} problem that more data do not cure

issues.why: In e2 the squared bias of OLS(z,f) exceeds half the MSE in only 33% (concave) and 38% (convex) of nonlinear cells, 50% of concave cells at Bernoulli(0.5) and 0% under Louvain clusters (results/summary/e2.csv); bias dominates mainly for sigmoid truth and p=0.1, so the abstract's unqualified statement holds only in part.

issues.quote: On Stanford3 (concave/linear truth) the coverage of the GATE under Bernoulli is 0.93/0.95 (HAC-2), 0.84/0.87 (cluster-robust), 0.82/0.83 (HC0); under Louvain resolution 1, 0.57/0.59 (HAC-2), 0.73/0.76 (cluster-robust)
issues.why: These values are not the coverage of OLS(z,f) in results/summary/e15.csv or results/tables/t19_coverage_expectation.csv (HAC-2 0.91/0.95 under Bernoulli and 0.46/0.46 under Louvain, cluster-robust 0.82/0.87 and 0.84/0.75, HC0 0.79/0.82); they equal the averages of OLS(z,f) and the correctly specified regression, from an ad hoc pivot that averaged over both estimators. The Louvain HAC-2 coverage of OLS(z,f) on Stanford3 is thus 0.46, not 0.57–0.59.

issues.quote: where the ratio estimator is biased upward ($+0.5$ to $+0.7$ full, $+0.28$ $\kappa$)
issues.why: In results/tables/t15_hajek.csv the estimable Bernoulli(0.8) step cells have HajekFull bias from +0.18 (BA, m=2) to +2.02 (ER, degree 8), not +0.5 to +0.7; the range was typed into a note of post_freeze.py rather than computed.

issues.quote: richer fits (penalised OLS, tuned boosting) do not help
issues.why: Tuned boosting beats OLS(z,f) in 21% of cells and has median RMSE ratio 0.40 with sigmoid truth at p=0.5 (Table 9); the body says this ('mostly with sigmoid truth'), so the abstract wording is stronger than the evidence but the qualification is in the paper.

issues.quote: the crossover strength scales as $n^{-0.49}d^{1.01}$ and the SD ratio as $d^{1.0}$
issues.why: The exponents come from one SBM family with linear truth and Bernoulli(0.5) (27 groups of e17), and gamma* is model-based and extrapolated above the simulated gamma grid in some cells; the abstract states the scaling without these restrictions (they appear only in Appendix D).

issues.quote: SD at $p=0.05$ relative to $p=0.5$: 2.32 and 2.21 against a predicted 2.29
issues.why: The p-dependence check compares single SD ratios with the prediction without any uncertainty; ratios of SDs from 400 draws carry a relative SE of about 5–7% (FINDINGS.md), so 'follows' is not shown to be distinguishable from small departures.

issues.quote: there the SD inflation goes with the few clusters and the cluster-level dependence of the treated share
issues.why: The explanation for the Stanford3 reversal is not isolated by an experiment (the proposed exposure-variation mechanism was refuted there); the paper concedes this in limitation (viii), so it is minor.

issues.quote: whose hubs break the homogeneous-degree argument
issues.why: The ego-Facebook departure from the 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) law is attributed to hubs without a test that varies hubs while holding the rest fixed.
The reason given for boosting's poor RMSE is plausible but no experiment separates extrapolation failure from variance or tuning.

issues.quote: 172 cells added after the first results
issues.why: The abstract says 172 cells were added after the first results, while Sec. 4 and Appendix D report 816 post-freeze cells (e11–e21; 1622 in all); 172 is only e11+e12.

issues.quote: were not changed to resolve ``unclear'' verdicts
issues.why: The record shows the H8a rule in findings.py rewritten one minute after it was first written, with the e2 graph RMSEs already inspected, replacing a rule without a 'refuted' branch (verdict 'unclear') by one that returns 'refuted'; the statement that thresholds were not changed to resolve unclear verdicts is therefore not accurate for H8a, although the underlying RMSE numbers are unaffected.

issues.quote: Richer fits were unpenalised, ridge/lasso-penalised or boosted with a small tuning grid; no other learner was tried.
issues.why: The covariate-selection regression estimator of Han & Ugander (2023), the most direct published competitor, and a Horvitz–Thompson estimator are not compared; the paper states the learner limitation, so it is minor.
Many reported numbers (SD ratios in Sec. 4.2, coverage means in Sec. 4.4, one-factor ranges, Sobol shares in text) are given without an uncertainty next to them.

presentation.why: Figure 1 is placed at 0.55 text width; panel titles, tick labels and legend are a few points high and hard to read in print.
Figure 6 (failure map) prints numbers in each heat-map cell at a very small size; the per-cell values are barely legible.

Captions and text carry repository paths and script names (results/summary/e2.csv, figures/scripts/make_tables.py, code/scripts/post_freeze.py), internal grid IDs e1–e21 and variable names (OLS_f, ORACLE_D in Table of Appendix E).
Appendix text refers to the making of the paper ('planning step of the pipeline', 'as reported by the simulation step', 'questions raised on the first version', 'The first-version statement ...').
Results paragraphs are very long and dense with numbers, grid IDs and hypothesis labels (H3g, H6c–e, e16, e17), which makes the main findings hard to extract.
There is no schematic of the estimand, estimator and the bias/variance mechanism; the first figure is a results plot.
Appendix pages 20–23 are mostly empty space around floats (page 22 holds a single small figure), a layout problem.

paper_mismatches.why: The two-hop cells of e7 (and e12, line 184) use gamma=1.0 and gamma2=1.0, not gamma=2 and gamma2=0.5 (results/summary/e7.csv: o_gamma=1, o_gamma2=1, GATE 3); the reported two-hop biases (-0.4 to -1.0) are for gamma2=1.

The equilibrium is approximated by 60 fixed-point iterations rather than the inverse; truth and outcomes use the same truncation (relative error about rho^60, 0.2% at rho=0.9), so results are internally consistent.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Each is produced by the script of the same name (tables: \texttt{make\_tables.py}) in \texttt{figures/scripts/}
paper_mismatches.why: The figure and table generators (figures/scripts/*.py, run_all.sh, make_tables.py of the figure step) and paper/check_numbers.py's inputs are referenced but figures/scripts is not in the delivery; the paper tables cannot be regenerated from delivered code.
OLS_quad also contains z*f (columns 1, z, f, f^2, zf); Appendix A lists this correctly but Appendix C names it OLS(z,f,f^2).

evaluation_errors.why: The Stanford3 coverage values for OLS(z,f) were read from a pivot table that averaged OLS(z,f) and the correctly specified regression (trajectory command at 08:52:33); e.g. Louvain HAC-2 coverage is reported as 0.57/0.59 whereas OLS(z,f) has 0.46/0.46 in results/summary/e15.csv. Reported numbers change; no main claim rests on them.

The closed-form prediction for synthetic graphs uses the degree sequence of the seed-0 graph of the family, while the simulated cells average over worlds with other graph draws; small, but the 'match within MC error' compares slightly different graphs.

problems.why: Figure/table scripts (figures/scripts/) are not delivered, so Tables 1-11 and all figures cannot be regenerated from the delivery; only the CSVs behind them can.
Per-replicate raw files are a separate release asset; RUNTIME.csv and coverage_analysis.py/world_uncertainty.py read results/raw, which is not delivered (compact parquet is).
Graph data default to a machine-specific absolute path (NETGATE_DATA default in REPRODUCE.md); the paper Makefile expects ../venue/iclr2027 style files that are not delivered.
matplotlib (needed for figures) is not in requirements.lock; full rerun needs about 67 CPU-hours.

process_notes: The first launch of e1-e9 (14:08) used a Louvain cache keyed by graph family only; it was torn down and all grids were rerun (stated in REPRODUCE.md).
All summaries e1-e12 were re-aggregated at 08:21 after the paper had first used them (aggregate.py gained bootstrap columns); e16 later confirmed e2 cells to the last digit.

post_freeze.py was rerun at 08:18 (with e13), regenerating hypotheses_postfreeze.csv and t14/t15 after the paper had first quoted them at 07:33; e14 regular-graph cells were rerun (08:11) after a division by zero in the log-degree baseline was fixed, before the paper used e14.
Post-freeze grids e11-e21 (816 cells) were added at the request of planning/review steps after the first results; the paper labels them as such.
Tool outputs are not stored in the record (only commands), and commands longer than 4000 characters are cut, so what was seen during the work can only be inferred from the commands.
Paper numbers were checked by a script (paper/check_numbers.py); during writing several quoted values were corrected to match the tables (e.g. HC0 coverage 0.67->0.66, bootstrap 0.84->0.83).

integrity.why: The studied estimator OLS(z,f) and all comparison specifications were fixed in the grid definitions before the runs; the commands that compare estimators on RMSE (e7, e12 pivots, C2c) only report them. The tuned GBM picks hyper-parameters by CV on observed outcomes, never on the exact GATE.

Metrics, truth and designs were not changed after results were seen. Decision thresholds for e1-e10 were written after the runs, which the paper states; one of them (H8a) was rewritten a minute after first writing to add a 'refuted' branch with the RMSE ordering known, which the paper's wording does not acknowledge (listed under issues), but it changes a verdict label, not any reported number. Post-freeze rules (e11/e12) were written at 07:12, before e12 (07:18) and e11 (07:24) were aggregated, and later edits only added labelled post-hoc rows. The outcomes.py fix (constant log-degree on regular graphs) led to a rerun of the affected e14 cells.

No estimator reads the exact GATE; the truth is used only in aggregate.py to score estimates. The 'oracle' regression uses the true exposure mapping by design and is labelled as a control, not as the method.

Every checked number traces to a result file written by a recorded script run. Two typed-in passages are not fabrications but misreadings: the Stanford3 coverage values came from a recorded pivot that averaged two estimators, and the '+0.5 to +0.7' Hajek bias was typed into a note. The run of factor_anova.py (t22) is not visible because its command is truncated in the record.
